1a.html:
Both are momentum-transfer pumps: an oil-vapour jet or a moving blade pushes each gas molecule towards the outlet. The push helps only if the molecule then reaches the outlet without hitting other molecules, that is in molecular flow, where the mean free path exceeds the pump dimensions:

\lambda\,[\mathrm{cm}] \approx \frac{5\times10^{-3}}{p\,[\mathrm{Torr}]}: \quad 50\ \mathrm{cm}\ \text{at}\ 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Torr}, \quad 50\ \mathrm{\mu m}\ \text{at}\ 1\ \mathrm{Torr}
  • Diffusion pump. Molecules wandering into the silicone-oil jet are driven down to the foreline. In viscous flow the dense gas scatters the jet and collisions return molecules upward, so the jet cannot hold the pressure difference; above about 5\times10^{-2} Torr it stops pumping.
  • Turbomolecular pump. At 24,000 rpm the blades move at about the molecular speed (461 m/s for air). A struck molecule must cross to the next stage without a collision. In viscous flow its momentum is randomised, compression collapses and drag overloads the rotor; hence the start below about 100 mTorr (\lambda \approx 0.5 mm, about the blade spacing).
  • So a roughing pump is used first, and a backing pump stays on the exhaust.
pts: States both are momentum-transfer pumps: an oil-vapour jet or a rotor blade gives individual molecules a directed velocity towards the outlet
Defines molecular flow as mean free path larger than the pump dimension (molecules hit walls, not each other), with \lambda \approx 5\times10^{-3}/p cm (p in Torr) or a number
Diffusion pump: in viscous flow gas collisions scatter the jet and return molecules, so the jet cannot hold the pressure ratio; upper limit about 5\times10^{-2} Torr

Turbo pump: blade speed comparable to molecular speed; a molecule must cross the stage gap without a collision; at high pressure momentum is randomised, compression lost and the rotor overloaded; started below about 100 mTorr
Concludes that a roughing pump is needed first and a backing (fore) pump on the exhaust, since neither works against viscous gas

1a.watch:
• "Analyze" asks for the reason (a collision-free path from the momentum source to the outlet), not only the pressure ranges.
  • In molecular flow the pumping speed is set by how many molecules wander into the inlet, the impingement flux p/\sqrt{2\pi mkT}; the pump does not push the gas as a fluid.
  • Turbo compression ratio rises exponentially with blade speed times \sqrt{M}, so \mathrm{H_2} is pumped poorly (about 10^3 against 10^9 for \mathrm{N_2}).
  • Oil backstreaming from a diffusion pump is worst in molecular flow, when no gas collisions stop the oil vapour; that is why it needs a cold cap and baffles. Do not mix this up with the reason the pump fails at high pressure.

1b.html:
Principle. The chamber reaches the pressure at which pumping balances the total gas load Q (Torr L/s):

P_{\mathrm{ult}} = \frac{Q}{S}

Q is the sum of real leaks, virtual leaks, outgassing, permeation and backstreaming. For 10^{-10} Torr with S = 500 L/s the whole load must be below 5\times10^{-8} Torr L/s, so each source is diagnosed (rate-of-rise test, He leak detector, residual-gas analyser) and fixed separately (slide 24).

Why baking is the key fix. With 1 \mathrm{m^2} of stainless steel wall, the slide 25 rates give Q = (2\times10^{-8})(10^4\ \mathrm{cm^2}) = 2\times10^{-4} mbar L/s unbaked, so P = 4\times10^{-7} mbar at 500 L/s. Electropolished and baked 30 h at 250 °C (4\times10^{-12}): Q = 4\times10^{-8} mbar L/s and P = 8\times10^{-11} mbar, true UHV. A cryopump then removes water fast and an ion pump holds about 10^{-11} Torr (slides 21-22).

Bulk outgassing and permeation (\mathrm{H_2} from steel, gas through elastomers and glass): metal seals, vacuum-fired steel, no polymers

1b.watch:
• "Synthesize a guide": the marks are in the links problem, origin, diagnosis, fix. A bare list of slide 24's four problems earns little.
  • The rate-of-rise test tells a leak from outgassing (Ohring): a leak rises linearly, outgassing levels off. A virtual leak behaves like outgassing and gives no He signal.
  • Baking works because the desorption residence time, \tau = \tau_0\exp(\Delta g^*_d/kT), falls steeply with temperature; water bound at room temperature leaves in hours at 200 °C instead of weeks.
  • The slide 25 rates are in \mathrm{mbar\,L\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} after 1 h in vacuum; they fall further with time, so the example pressures are upper estimates.

1c.html:
Stoichiometry is lost because the vapour composition differs from the source composition, and because the substrate does not keep every species that arrives.

Alloys: fractionation. The constituents evaporate almost independently, as atoms, each at its own vapour pressure. In the melt the vapour pressure follows Raoult's law with an activity coefficient, p_B = \gamma_B X_B p_B^0, so with the Hertz-Knudsen rate

\frac{\Phi_A}{\Phi_B} = \frac{\gamma_A X_A\, p_A^0}{\gamma_B X_B\, p_B^0}\left(\frac{M_B}{M_A}\right)^{1/2}

The more volatile component is enriched in the vapour and the film. Example: at 1350 K, p_{\mathrm{Al}}^0/p_{\mathrm{Cu}}^0 \approx 5, so an Al-2 wt% Cu film needs a melt of Al:Cu about 15:1 (13.6 wt% Cu). As Al is lost the melt and the flux ratio drift, so the film is graded through its thickness.

Compounds: dissociation. Few compounds evaporate as molecules (SiO, \mathrm{MgF_2}, \mathrm{B_2O_3}). Most dissociate, \mathrm{MX(s)} \to \mathrm{M(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{X_2(g)}:

  • the gaseous non-metal (\mathrm{S_2}, \mathrm{Se_2}, \mathrm{As_2}) has a low sticking coefficient and is partly pumped away, so deposits are metal-rich (Ga-rich GaAs; CdS and CdTe need separate sources);
  • dioxides lose oxygen to lower oxides, \mathrm{SiO_2} \to \mathrm{SiO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}, giving discoloured, oxygen-deficient \mathrm{SiO}_x or \mathrm{TiO}_x.

At the substrate. A hot substrate re-evaporates the volatile species, and residual \mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{H_2O} or \mathrm{N_2} arriving at F_i = p_i/\sqrt{2\pi m_i kT} are built in.

Control: separate sources with their own rate monitors, flash or wire-fed evaporation, reactive evaporation in \mathrm{O_2}, or an overpressure of the volatile species (As for GaAs).
pts: States the cause: the vapour composition differs from the source, and not every arriving species sticks
Alloys evaporate atom by atom, each at its own vapour pressure, with Raoult's law p_B = \gamma_B X_B p_B^0
Gives the flux ratio \Phi_A/\Phi_B with the (M_B/M_A)^{1/2} factor; the more volatile component is enriched in the film
Explains source depletion: melt composition and flux ratio change with time, so the film is graded (example Al-Cu or Ni-Cr)
Compounds dissociate, \mathrm{MX} \to \mathrm{M(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{X_2(g)}; the volatile non-metal sticks poorly and is pumped away, giving metal-rich films (Ga-rich GaAs)
Oxides decompose to lower oxides (\mathrm{SiO_2} \to \mathrm{SiO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}), giving oxygen-deficient films; only a few (SiO, \mathrm{MgF_2}) evaporate unchanged
Substrate effects (re-evaporation at high T_{\mathrm{sub}}, residual-gas pick-up) and at least one remedy (separate sources, flash evaporation, reactive evaporation, As overpressure)

1c.watch:
• "Investigate the physical processes": name each one (fractionation, depletion, dissociation, low sticking or re-evaporation), not only "the composition changes".
  • The flux ratio holds only at the first instant; X and \gamma change as the melt is depleted, and activity coefficients are rarely known.
  • The X_{A_A} term crossed out on slide 32 for a pure source is exactly the alloy correction: for an alloy keep the activity.
  • Sputtering avoids fractionation: the target surface reaches a steady state and the film reproduces the target composition.

2a.html:
An electron obeys the Lorentz force (slide 11):

m_e\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}), \qquad q = -e

The electric force does work; the magnetic force is perpendicular to \mathbf{v}, so it bends the path without changing the speed.

  1. E only (or v along both fields): force -e\mathbf{E}, opposite to the field. The electron accelerates in a straight line from cathode to anode, gaining energy eV, enough to ionise Ar (15.7 eV).
  2. B only, v at angle θ to B: v\cos\theta along B is unchanged; v\sin\theta gives a circle of radius r = m_e v\sin\theta/(eB) at the cyclotron frequency \omega_c = eB/m_e. The path is a helix of constant pitch wound on the field lines, so off-axis electrons are not lost to the walls. For a 10 eV electron in 0.03 T, r \approx 0.36 mm and f_c \approx 840 MHz; an Ar ion's radius is about 270 times larger, so ions are hardly deflected.
  3. E parallel to B: the same helix, but the pitch grows as E accelerates the electron along B.
  4. E perpendicular to B (magnetron): E pulls the electron off the cathode, B bends it back, giving a cycloid that hops along the target and drifts along \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B} at E/B.

Consequence: electrons stay near the target far longer and make many more ionising collisions, so the plasma is denser, the rate higher and the pressure can be lower (slides 11-12).
pts: Lorentz force \mathbf{F} = -e(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}); magnetic force perpendicular to \mathbf{v}, does no work
E only: straight-line acceleration toward the anode, opposite to E, gaining energy eV
B only: helix of constant pitch; gyroradius r = m_e v\sin\theta/(eB) and cyclotron frequency \omega_c = eB/m_e
E parallel to B: helix whose pitch increases
E perpendicular to B: cycloidal hopping near the cathode with drift along \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}, electrons trapped
Consequence: longer electron path, more ionisation, denser plasma at lower pressure (magnetron); ions too heavy to be confined

2a.watch:
• Put the minus sign on the electron charge: the force is opposite to E, and the drift direction on slide 11 (to the right for E down and B into the page) only comes out with q = -e.
  • The \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B} drift is the same for electrons and ions, but ions have gyroradii of centimetres, larger than the plasma region, so only electrons are trapped.
  • Ohring gives f_c = 2.8 MHz per gauss; 0.03 T is 300 G, which gives 840 MHz.

2b.html:
When a discharge ion hits the target (cathode):

  1. Acceleration. \mathrm{Ar^+} falls through the cathode sheath (dark space) and arrives with a few hundred eV (target at about −500 V on a magnetron, slide 12).
  2. Neutralisation. Within a few ångströms it captures an electron from the target (about 10^{-15} s), so it strikes, and reflects, mostly as a neutral.
  3. Momentum transfer. An elastic collision passes the fraction 4M_1M_2/(M_1+M_2)^2 of its energy to a target atom (0.95 for Ar on Cu).
  4. Outcome by energy. Below a few eV the ion adsorbs or reflects. Above the 10 to 30 eV threshold (slide 8) a collision cascade turns momentum back to the surface and ejects atoms: sputtering, about 0.8 (Si) to 3.2 (Au) atoms per ion at 1 keV. Above about 10 keV the ion is mostly implanted.
  5. Emission. Sputtered atoms (mostly neutral, 3 to 10 eV, cosine-like spread, slide 6); reflected Ar neutrals; secondary electrons, accelerated into the plasma to ionise Ar and sustain the discharge; some negative ions and photons.
  6. Left in the target. Trapped Ar, displaced atoms, an altered layer enriched in the low-yield element (slide 9), and heat (most of the ion energy), removed by water cooling.

At the growing film the same events occur at lower energy: higher adatom mobility, resputtering, densification and gas incorporation.
pts: Ion acceleration across the cathode sheath to hundreds of eV; neutralisation by electron capture just before impact
Momentum (not heat) transfer in elastic collisions, energy fraction 4M_1M_2/(M_1+M_2)^2
Energy regimes: adsorption or reflection at low energy; sputtering above the 10 to 30 eV threshold by a collision cascade; implantation at high energy (above about 10 keV)
Emitted species: sputtered neutral atoms (few eV), reflected neutrals, secondary electrons that sustain the discharge, negative ions or photons
Changes in the target: gas implantation, displacement damage, altered (preferentially sputtered) layer, heating needing water cooling
Labelled sketch of the interactions, or the same processes named at the growing film (mobility, resputtering, densification, gas incorporation)

2b.watch:
• Sputtering is a momentum-transfer process, not evaporation: the ejected atoms carry 3 to 10 eV, far above thermal energies (about 0.1 eV from an evaporation source).
  • Most of the bombarding energy becomes target heat; only a small fraction goes into sputtered atoms, which is why targets are water-cooled.
  • Ohring's sticking curve has a minimum of about 0.2 near 20 eV: below threshold ions stick, in the sputtering range many reflect.

2c.html:
Both sputter the target with \mathrm{Ar^+} ions from a glow discharge by momentum transfer (slide 2); they differ in how the target is powered (slide 3).

AspectDC sputteringRF sputtering
Operating principletarget is the cathode at a constant negative voltage (about −1 to −3 kV diode, about −500 V magnetron); chamber and substrate are the grounded anode; \mathrm{Ar^+} crosses the cathode dark space13.56 MHz voltage through a matching network and blocking capacitor; electrons follow the field, ions cannot, so the target self-biases negative and is bombarded for nearly the whole cycle; small target, large grounded area so only the target sputters
Target materialconductors only: on an insulator the ion charge cannot drain, the surface charges positive and the discharge stopsany material: metals, semiconductors and insulators (\mathrm{SiO_2}, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, ZnO, PZT), since RF couples through the target's capacitance
Deposition ratehigher for metals; simple, cheap supply; about 1 μm/min for Al with a magnetronlower: less power reaches the ions, and brittle, poorly conducting ceramic targets crack at high power
Plasma behaviourglow sustained by secondary electrons from the target; plasma near the cathode; a diode runs at about 75 to 140 mTorr (rate peak near 110 mTorr, slide 10); arcs on poisoned targetselectrons oscillating in the field gain energy and ionise without secondary electrons; more efficient ionisation (electron density 10^9 to 10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}); plasma fills the chamber; runs at 0.5 to 10 mTorr, so less gas scattering and incorporation

Why DC fails on insulators. The target must pass the ion current: V = \rho j d. For quartz (\rho \approx 10^{16}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{cm}, j = 1\ \mathrm{mA\,cm^{-2}}, d = 1 mm) this is 10^{12} V, so the field collapses.

Conclusion. DC (with a magnetron) is the fast, cheap choice for metals; RF is needed for insulating targets, at higher cost and lower rate. Reactive DC sputtering of a metal target is the usual industrial alternative for oxides and nitrides.
pts: DC principle: target is the cathode at constant negative voltage, substrate and chamber the anode; \mathrm{Ar^+} accelerated across the dark space

RF principle: 13.56 MHz through a matching network and blocking capacitor; electrons mobile, ions not, so the target self-biases negative and is sputtered for most of the cycle; small target relative to grounded area
Target compatibility: DC conductors only (charge build-up on insulators stops sputtering, V = \rho j d); RF any material including oxides and nitrides
Deposition rate: DC higher for metals and cheaper (especially with a magnetron); RF lower, ceramic targets limit power

Plasma behaviour: DC sustained by secondary electrons, higher pressure for a diode (about 100 mTorr), arcing risk; RF electrons gain energy in the oscillating field, more efficient ionisation, operation at about 0.5 to 10 mTorr
Conclusion or applications: DC for metals, RF for insulators; cost and complexity of RF

2c.watch:
• Without the self-bias an AC electrode would sputter only half the time, and the substrate as much as the target.
  • "Plasma behaviour" wants the ionisation mechanism (secondary electrons against oscillating electrons) and the operating pressure, not just "RF prevents charge build-up".
  • Ohring notes that RF sputtering of compound targets tends to give metal-rich (oxygen-deficient) films.

3a.html:
Set-up. A negative bias -V_b on the substrate (typically −50 to −300 V, against −1 to −3 kV on a diode target) accelerates \mathrm{Ar^+} from the plasma onto the growing film. At low pressure there are few collisions in the anode sheath, so ions arrive with nearly the full energy e(V_p + V_b) and the effect of bias is strong. Bias is a process parameter that sets microstructure, stress and impurity content (slide 5).

Prediction as V_b is raised:

  1. Small to moderate bias (tens to about 100 V):
    • sputter-cleans the substrate and removes adsorbed \mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{N_2}, \mathrm{H_2O}: better adhesion and purity, lower resistivity (Ta, W, Cr, Au);
    • raises adatom mobility and renucleation: porous, voided Zone 1 columns give way to a dense, fine-grained structure, as at higher T_s/T_m (slides 14-15, printed 15-16);
    • resputters loosely bound atoms at corners and peaks: smoother film, better step coverage (Al);
    • atomic peening makes the stress compressive.
  2. High bias:
    • resputtering grows, so the net deposition rate falls (and can reach zero, net etching);
    • trapped Ar rises roughly as V_b^2; displacement damage, lattice expansion and large compressive stress cause hardening, cracking or delamination;
    • extra substrate heating; in alloys, preferential resputtering shifts the composition.

Conclusion: film quality improves with bias up to an optimum moderate value, then degrades, while the deposition rate falls throughout.
pts: Bias mechanism: negative substrate voltage accelerates plasma ions onto the growing film; at low pressure few sheath collisions, so ions arrive with nearly full energy
Prediction: surface cleaning and desorption of impurity gases give better adhesion, purity and lower resistivity
Prediction: higher adatom mobility and renucleation give dense, fine-grained films without voided Zone 1 columns
Prediction: resputtering of loosely bound atoms gives smoother films and better step coverage
Prediction: compressive stress from atomic peening
High bias: resputtering lowers the net deposition rate; Ar incorporation (about V_b^2), defects and excessive stress
Conclusion: an optimum moderate bias for quality, with the rate falling as bias rises

3a.watch:
• "Predict" wants the trend with V_b and its reason, including the downside at high bias, not just a list of benefits.
  • Ion energy is set by the potential difference between plasma and substrate, V_p + V_b; the plasma potential alone (5 to 10 V in DC systems) already gives mild bombardment of a grounded substrate.
  • Where the optimum lies depends on the metal and on ion flux; the slides give no value, so state it as a trend.

3b.html:
Process. A metal target (Ti, Al, Ta, Si) is sputtered in Ar mixed with a reactive gas (\mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{N_2}, \mathrm{CH_4}, \mathrm{H_2S}). Metal atoms react with the gas, mainly on the substrate, giving compound films such as TiN, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, \mathrm{SiO_2}, TaN, TiC (slide 13, printed 14). Pure, ductile metal targets are easier to make than brittle compound ones, DC power can be used, and the gas flow tunes the composition (Ta, \mathrm{Ta_2N}, then TaN as p_{\mathrm{N_2}} rises).

Gas balance. The reactive gas fed in is either gettered by fresh metal on the target and substrate or pumped away:

Q_r = Q_{\mathrm{target}} + Q_{\mathrm{substrate}} + P_r S

Hysteresis.

  1. Metallic mode A (low Q_r). Sputtered metal getters all the gas, so P_r \approx 0 and the pressure stays at its Ar value. The target is metallic, the rate high, the film a doped metal.
  2. Avalanche at Q_r^*. Gettering can no longer keep up; compound starts to cover the target. Compounds sputter far more slowly than metals (S_c \ll S_m), so less metal is sputtered, less gas is gettered and P_r rises, which covers more target: positive feedback.
  3. Poisoned (compound) mode B. The pressure jumps to the linear branch P = P_{\mathrm{Ar}} + P_r, the rate collapses, and the target voltage usually drops (compounds emit more secondary electrons, lowering the plasma impedance).
  4. Return. On lowering Q_r, the compound layer must be sputtered away at the low yield S_c, so the system stays poisoned down to a much lower flow before snapping back. Two stable states with abrupt switching form the loop.

Consequences and control. Stoichiometric films at high rate lie in the unstable transition region. Remedies: closed-loop control of P_r (optical emission, target voltage), high pumping speed S (shrinks the loop), reactive gas fed near the substrate, and pulsed-DC or dual magnetrons to stop arcing on poisoned targets.
pts: Reactive sputtering defined: metal target in Ar plus reactive gas, compound formed on the substrate, with examples (TiN, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, \mathrm{SiO_2}, TaN)
Advantages: pure ductile metal targets, DC power, composition tuned by reactive gas flow
Gas balance: gas gettered by target and substrate or pumped, Q_r = Q_t + Q_s + P_r S
Metallic mode: gas fully gettered, pressure unchanged, high rate, metallic target, doped-metal film
Transition: target poisoning with S_c \ll S_m, less gettering, positive feedback, abrupt jump in pressure and fall in rate (and target voltage)
Return path: target stays poisoned until a lower flow, so two stable states and a hysteresis loop
Sketch of pressure (or rate) against reactive gas flow showing the loop
Consequence and control: desired stoichiometric high-rate region is unstable; feedback control of P_r, high pumping speed, pulsed power against arcing

3b.watch:
• The loop is in pressure, deposition rate and target voltage at once; draw at least one with both branches and arrows.
  • The jump is triggered by compound on the target, not by compound on the substrate.
  • Insulating compound on the target also charges up and arcs, and coating of the chamber shrinks the anode ("disappearing anode"); pulsed DC at tens of kHz or AC dual magnetrons solve both.

3c.html:
The structure zone model (SZM) predicts film microstructure from the homologous temperature T_s/T_m (both in K). Activation energies for surface and bulk diffusion scale with T_m, so T_s/T_m sets adatom mobility; at low T_s/T_m shadowing by surface bumps dominates. Movchan-Demchishin (evaporated coatings) has three zones; Thornton (sputtered coatings) adds an Ar pressure axis and a transition zone T.

ZoneT_s/T_mControlling processStructure and properties
1below 0.3shadowing, little adatom diffusionporous, tapered columns with domed tops and voided boundaries; rough, low density, weak
T (Thornton)between Zones 1 and 2limited surface diffusion plus energetic bombardmentdense fibrous grains, smooth, hard, no voids
20.3 to 0.5surface diffusioncolumnar grains with dense boundaries; column width grows with T_s/T_m; faceted surface
3above 0.5bulk diffusion, recrystallisationequiaxed grains, bulk-like density and properties

Temperature. Raising T_s/T_m moves the film from Zone 1 through T and 2 to 3: voids close, grains grow and become equiaxed, and properties approach bulk values.

Pressure (Thornton). High Ar pressure (about 30 mTorr, mean free path about 2 mm, far below the target-substrate distance) scatters and thermalises the sputtered atoms. They arrive slowly and obliquely, shadowing grows and porous Zone 1 extends to higher T_s/T_m; such films are usually tensile. At low pressure (about 1 mTorr) energetic atoms and reflected Ar neutrals bombard the film, densifying it and widening Zone T; such films are usually compressive.

Examples. Al at room temperature, 300/933 \approx 0.32: Zone 2 columns. Ni at room temperature, 300/1728 \approx 0.17: fine Zone 1 or T structure. Electron-beam YSZ thermal-barrier coatings are deliberately Zone 1 (porous columns) for strain tolerance.
pts: Defines the homologous temperature T_s/T_m (K) and why it controls adatom mobility (activation energies scale with T_m)
Zone 1 (T_s/T_m below 0.3): shadowing and limited diffusion give porous, tapered columns with voided boundaries and low density
Zone T (Thornton): dense, fibrous grains with a smooth surface, between Zones 1 and 2
Zone 2 (0.3 to 0.5): surface-diffusion-controlled columnar grains with dense boundaries; grain width grows with temperature
Zone 3 (above 0.5): bulk diffusion and recrystallisation give equiaxed grains with bulk-like properties
Pressure: high Ar pressure scatters atoms, lowering energy and making arrival oblique, so Zone 1 extends to higher T_s/T_m; low pressure means bombardment and densification
Property consequence: high-pressure porous films in tension, low-pressure dense films in compression
Gives examples with T_s/T_m values (Al at room temperature about 0.32, Ni about 0.17, porous YSZ thermal-barrier coatings)

4a.html:
Framework. A film nucleus on a substrate (capillarity model, Ohring) has the barrier and density

\Delta G^* = \frac{16\pi\gamma_f^3}{3(\Delta G_v + \Delta G_s)^2}\cdot\frac{2 - 3\cos\theta + \cos^3\theta}{4}, \qquad N^* = n_s\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G^*}{kT}\right)

with \gamma_s = \gamma_i + \gamma_f\cos\theta (Young). Each substrate property enters a different term.

  1. Surface energy, \gamma_s, sets \theta. High-\gamma_s substrates (clean metals, 1 to 3 \mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}; semiconductors with dangling bonds) are wetted, \gamma_s > \gamma_i + \gamma_f, \theta \to 0: no barrier, Frank-van der Merwe layers. Low-\gamma_s oxides and alkali halides give \theta > 0: a barrier and Volmer-Weber islands (metals on \mathrm{SiO_2}, Ag on NaCl).
  2. Crystal lattice. The misfit f = (a_s - a_f)/a_f sets \gamma_i (low if coherent) and the strain energy of the nucleus, \Delta G_s > 0, which raises \Delta G^*. Small f: pseudomorphic epitaxy up to h_c \sim 1/f (about 100 Å at 1%); a few percent: Stranski-Krastanov (Ge on Si, 4%); large: islands, polycrystalline or textured film. Steps and dislocations are preferred sites.
  3. Electrical conductivity reflects the bond type. Metals bind metal adatoms strongly; covalent semiconductors offer directional dangling bonds that template epitaxy; ionic insulators bind weakly, so adatoms cluster at defects. An insulator also keeps charge from a plasma or e-beam, which alters \Delta G^*, and cannot be DC-biased; a conductor drains charge and can be biased.

Collective effect. GaAs on Ge (covalent, matched): FvM epitaxy; Ge on Si (4% misfit): SK; Au on NaCl (ionic, low \gamma_s): oriented VW islands; Cu on amorphous \mathrm{SiO_2}: polycrystalline islands needing a Ta or TiN adhesion layer. Surface energy decides the mode, the lattice the orientation, strain and defects, and conductivity the bonding and charging; a low T_{\mathrm{sub}} or high flux (small \delta_{ad}) can override all three.
pts: Nucleation barrier with the wetting factor (2 - 3\cos\theta + \cos^3\theta)/4 and Young's equation; nucleus density N^* \propto \exp(-\Delta G^*/kT)
Surface energy: high \gamma_s (metals, clean semiconductors) wets, FvM, no barrier; low \gamma_s (oxides, halides) gives \theta > 0 and VW islands, with an example
Lattice misfit: sets \gamma_i and strain energy; small misfit pseudomorphic epitaxy (h_c \sim 1/f), moderate misfit SK, large misfit islands or polycrystalline film
Conductivity as a marker of bond type (metallic, covalent, ionic) and adatom binding, with its effect on wetting and nucleation
Charging of insulating substrates by plasma or beams alters nucleation and prevents DC bias; conductors drain charge and can be biased
Evaluates the collective effect with at least two examples (GaAs on Ge, Ge on Si, Au on NaCl, Cu on \mathrm{SiO_2}) and notes that kinetics can override

• "Electrical conductivity" is not in the slides' growth-mode lectures; it matters through bonding (it tracks the electronic structure that sets \gamma_s and adatom binding) and through charging. State that link explicitly.
  • Young's equation holds strictly for liquids (slide 3 of the second epitaxy deck); for solids use it as an energy argument.
  • Do not write \gamma_s < \gamma_i + \gamma_f for wetting: layer growth needs \gamma_s larger than the sum.
  • Selective CVD is another substrate effect: \mathrm{WF_6} deposits W on exposed Si but not on neighbouring insulator surfaces (Ohring).

4b.fix: Slide 6 writes the \mathrm{SiCl_4} route as \mathrm{SiCl_4(g) \rightarrow Si(s) + 2Cl_2(g)}. \mathrm{SiCl_4} is very stable (standard free energy of formation about -617\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} at 298 K), so direct decomposition to \mathrm{Cl_2} is negligible at CVD temperatures. The working reaction is hydrogen reduction, \mathrm{SiCl_4 + 2H_2 \rightarrow Si + 4HCl} at about 1200 °C (Ohring eq. 6-3), which is why Si epitaxy uses \mathrm{H_2} as the carrier gas.
4b.html:
CVD grows a film by a heterogeneous, thermally activated reaction of volatile precursors on the hot substrate (slide 2: reactions are usually "pyrolytic"). Four reaction types:

TypeWhat happensExampleAbout
Pyrolysisheat alone breaks a hydride, carbonyl or organometallic\mathrm{SiH_4 \rightarrow Si + 2H_2}; \mathrm{Ni(CO)_4 \rightarrow Ni + 4CO}650; 180 °C
Reduction\mathrm{H_2} strips a halide\mathrm{SiCl_4 + 2H_2 \rightarrow Si + 4HCl}; \mathrm{WF_6 + 3H_2 \rightarrow W + 6HF}1200; 300 °C
Oxidation\mathrm{O_2} or \mathrm{CO_2} forms an oxide\mathrm{SiH_4 + O_2 \rightarrow SiO_2 + 2H_2}; \mathrm{2AlCl_3 + 3H_2 + 3CO_2 \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 3CO + 6HCl}450; 1000 °C
Compound formationtwo precursors give a carbide, nitride or III-V\mathrm{TiCl_4 + CH_4 \rightarrow TiC + 4HCl}; \mathrm{3SiH_2Cl_2 + 4NH_3 \rightarrow Si_3N_4 + 6H_2 + 6HCl}; \mathrm{(CH_3)_3Ga + AsH_3 \rightarrow GaAs + 3CH_4}1000; 750; 650 to 750 °C

Precursor selection.

  • Volatile at low temperature: a gas (\mathrm{SiH_4}) or a bubbler liquid whose temperature sets p_{\mathrm{react}} (slides 6-7: \mathrm{SiH_2Cl_2}, \mathrm{SiHCl_3}, \mathrm{SiCl_4} boil near 8, 32, 57 °C).
  • Only volatile by-products (\mathrm{H_2}, HCl, HF, CO, \mathrm{CH_4}), so the film stays pure.
  • Pyrolysis needs weakly bonded molecules (hydrides, carbonyls, metal-organics): low T, but toxic or pyrophoric, prone to gas-phase powder and C or H pick-up.
  • Reduction uses cheap, pure, stable halides; HCl by-product can etch the film back, which favours clean epitaxy.
  • Compound formation needs two precursors of matched reactivity; their flow ratio sets the stoichiometry.

Process temperature. T must make \Delta G negative and overcome the activation energy of the surface step (k_s \propto e^{-Q_r^*/kT}). Stronger bonds need higher T: Si sources run \mathrm{SiH_4} < \mathrm{SiH_2Cl_2} < \mathrm{SiHCl_3} < \mathrm{SiCl_4}, the knee moving up from about 900 °C (slide 21, printed 22). The substrate limits the choice: over Al metallisation only low-temperature routes such as \mathrm{SiH_4 + O_2} (450 °C) or \mathrm{WF_6} (300 °C) fit; epitaxial Si uses chloride reduction at 1050 to 1200 °C. Plasma activation (PECVD, slide 52, printed 53) or organometallics lower T further, at the cost of hydrogen or carbon in the film.
pts: Defines CVD as a thermally activated heterogeneous reaction of volatile precursors, with volatile by-products leaving
Pyrolysis: thermal decomposition of hydrides, carbonyls or organometallics, with a balanced example and temperature (\mathrm{SiH_4} at about 650 °C or \mathrm{Ni(CO)_4} at 180 °C)
Reduction: \mathrm{H_2} reduction of a halide, balanced example (\mathrm{SiCl_4} at about 1200 °C or \mathrm{WF_6} at 300 °C)
Oxidation: balanced example (\mathrm{SiH_4 + O_2} at 450 °C or \mathrm{AlCl_3/CO_2/H_2} to \mathrm{Al_2O_3} at 1000 °C)
Compound formation: two precursors give carbide, nitride or III-V, balanced example (TiC, \mathrm{Si_3N_4} or GaAs by MOCVD)
Precursor criteria: volatility (gas or bubbler vapour pressure), clean volatile by-products, reactivity matched to the reaction type, with safety, purity or cost trade-off
Temperature: must make \Delta G < 0 and activate k_s; weaker bonds give lower T, e.g. Si sources \mathrm{SiH_4} < \mathrm{SiH_2Cl_2} < \mathrm{SiHCl_3} < \mathrm{SiCl_4}
Substrate or device limits the temperature (450 °C oxide over Al, 1050 to 1200 °C for epitaxy); plasma or organometallic precursors lower it

4c.html:
Principle. ALD is CVD split into sequential, self-limiting surface reactions. The precursors never meet in the gas: they are pulsed in turn through fast valves, with inert-gas purges between (slide 55, printed 56). For ZnS, \mathrm{ZnCl_2 + H_2S \rightarrow ZnS + 2HCl} (slide 56, printed 57):

  1. Precursor 1 pulse: \mathrm{ZnCl_2} chemisorbs on the surface sites. It attaches to the surface but not to itself, so adsorption stops when the sites are full: a saturated monolayer.
  2. Purge: Ar or \mathrm{N_2} sweeps out the excess precursor.
  3. Precursor 2 pulse: \mathrm{H_2S} reacts only with the adsorbed layer, giving one monolayer of ZnS and volatile HCl, and leaves a fresh reactive surface.
  4. Purge, then repeat.

Growth mechanism compared with CVD. In CVD the reactants flow together and continuously, and the rate is set by flux and temperature (Grove: F = k_s h_G C_G/(k_s + h_G)), so it depends on T, p_{\mathrm{react}}, flow and position in the reactor. In ALD each half-reaction saturates, so the deposit per cycle is fixed by the surface chemistry, not by dose or flux, inside a temperature window (too cold: condensation or incomplete reaction; too hot: precursor decomposition, which is CVD again).

Thickness control. CVD: thickness = rate × time, about 0.1 to 1 μm/min (slide 21, printed 22), so uniformity rests on uniform T and gas supply. ALD: digital, thickness = N × growth per cycle (at most one monolayer, typically about 0.1 nm), so sub-nm control, ±2 % repeatability without feedback, and uniform, pinhole-free coating of deep trenches. The cost is low rate. Hence ALD makes \mathrm{HfO_2} gate dielectrics and coats 6 nm FinFET and gate-all-around channels (slides 56-57, printed 57-58).
pts: ALD principle: precursors introduced sequentially in separate pulses, separated by inert-gas purges, never mixing in the gas

Self-limiting chemisorption: precursor 1 saturates the surface sites at one monolayer; precursor 2 reacts only with that layer (example \mathrm{ZnCl_2/H_2S \rightarrow ZnS + 2HCl}, or TMA/water for \mathrm{Al_2O_3})
Labelled cycle sketch: dose, purge, dose, purge, repeat

Growth mechanism vs CVD: CVD reactants simultaneous and continuous, rate set by flux and temperature (transport or reaction limited); ALD growth per cycle fixed by surface saturation within a temperature window
Thickness control: ALD digital, t = N \times GPC (about 0.1 nm per cycle), sub-nm precision; CVD thickness = rate × time, sensitive to T, pressure and flow
Consequences: best conformality, pinhole-free, ±2 % repeatability, but slow; CVD much faster (about 0.1 to 1 μm/min)
Application: \mathrm{HfO_2} gate dielectric, FinFET or gate-all-around transistors

• Four panels of a surface: precursor 1 adsorbed as one saturated layer with excess in the gas; purge; precursor 2 reacting, by-product leaving; purge leaving one monolayer of product.
  • Label the self-limiting step, the purges and "repeat N cycles, t = N \times GPC".

4c.watch:
• "Self-limiting" is the key word: without it ALD is just pulsed CVD.
  • Growth per cycle is usually less than a full monolayer, because bulky precursor ligands block neighbouring sites.
  • Above the ALD window the precursor decomposes on its own, the growth stops being self-limiting and conformality is lost.
  • Ohring calls the epitaxial version atomic layer epitaxy (ALE, "digital epitaxy"); the slide title gives both names.

5a.html:
Quantum confinement is the restriction of electron (and hole) motion to a region comparable with their de Broglie wavelength, or, in a semiconductor, smaller than the exciton Bohr radius a_{ex}. The energy levels inside then become discrete instead of forming continuous bands.

Why the levels separate. A band holds as many states per sublevel as there are atoms. In a bulk solid the spacing \Delta E is negligible and the band is continuous; in a particle of a few hundred to a few thousand atoms the splits are distinct, and \Delta E grows as the volume shrinks. The particle-in-a-box model gives the scale:

E_n = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8 m^* L^2}

The energies rise as 1/L^2: for L = 2 nm and m^* = 0.13\,m_e (electrons in CdSe), E_1 \approx 0.72 eV.

Effect on the band gap. The lowest conduction-band state moves up and the highest valence-band state moves down, so the gap widens as the particle shrinks (Brus model, R = particle radius):

E_g(R) = E_g(\text{bulk}) + \frac{h^2}{8R^2}\left(\frac{1}{m_e^*} + \frac{1}{m_h^*}\right) - \frac{1.8\,e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r R}

The last term is the electron-hole Coulomb attraction. Confinement is strong when R < a_{ex} (CdS 3 nm, GaAs 11 nm, PbS 18 nm).

Consequence. Absorption and emission shift to shorter wavelengths (blue shift). From the CdSe spectra on the slides, the first absorption peak is at about 2.1 eV for 4 nm and about 2.6 eV for 2 nm particles, against 1.74 eV for bulk CdSe. The gap, and so the colour, is tuned by size alone.
pts: Defines quantum confinement: carriers confined to a size comparable with their de Broglie wavelength or the exciton Bohr radius, so the levels become discrete
Explains the splitting: one state per atom in each sublevel, so the spacing \Delta E grows as the volume shrinks
Particle in a box, E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2: confinement energy rises as 1/L^2
States that the band gap widens as the size falls (conduction edge up, valence edge down), with the Brus expression or an equivalent argument
Strong confinement when R < a_{ex}, with a value (for example CdS 3 nm, GaAs 11 nm)
Blue shift of absorption and emission, with an example (CdSe 1.74 eV bulk against about 2.1 to 2.6 eV for 4 to 2 nm dots)
Diagram of bulk bands against discrete levels with a wider gap

• Energy axis; bulk: continuous valence and conduction bands with E_g.
  • Nanoparticle: discrete levels at the band edges and a larger E_g; a smaller particle, a larger gap still.
  • The photon arrow across the gap, labelled "blue shift" for smaller particles.

  • Do not say the gap shrinks: smaller particles always have the larger gap.

5c.html:
Nanomaterials behave differently because their size is comparable with the electron wavelength (quantum confinement) and much smaller than the wavelength of light (surface plasmons in metals).

Quantum dots. In a semiconductor nanocrystal smaller than the exciton Bohr radius, electrons and holes are confined in all three directions. The bands split into discrete, atom-like levels and the gap widens as the dot shrinks (particle in a box, E \propto 1/L^2). Hence:

  • Size-tunable colour. Absorption and emission blue-shift as the size falls. For CdSe the first absorption peak moves from 1.74 eV in bulk to about 2.1 eV at 4 nm and 2.6 eV at 2 nm (from the slide spectra), so one material emits from red to blue.
  • Discrete absorption peaks (exciton transitions) replace the smooth absorption edge of the bulk.
  • Narrow, bright, photostable emission, excited by any photon above the gap, so one UV source excites dots of every colour: biological tagging, QLED displays and lasers.

Metal nanoparticles show surface plasmon resonance: light drives a collective oscillation of the conduction electrons, so 10 to 20 nm gold absorbs near 520 nm and looks red, not golden.
pts: Gives the reasons: size comparable with the electron wavelength or exciton Bohr radius (confinement) and smaller than the light wavelength
In quantum dots three-dimensional confinement gives discrete, atom-like levels and a wider gap as the size falls
Size-tunable absorption and emission with a blue shift for smaller dots, with an example (CdSe red to blue, or 1.74 eV to about 2.1 to 2.6 eV)
Discrete exciton absorption peaks instead of a continuous edge
Narrow, bright emission from one excitation source, with an application (bio-tagging, displays)
Surface plasmon resonance of metal nanoparticles (gold red, absorbing near 520 nm)

5d.html:
NAPT kills tumour cells with heat made by gold nanoshells that absorb near-infrared (NIR) light, while healthy tissue, which NIR crosses safely, stays cool.

Role of the nanoshells

  • A nanoshell is a dielectric core (silica, about 120 nm) coated with a thin gold shell (about 10 nm).
  • The core-to-shell ratio tunes its plasmon resonance: a thin shell moves it from 520 nm (solid gold) to about 800 nm, inside the NIR tissue window (about 650 to 900 nm), where blood and water absorb little and light penetrates centimetres.
  • At resonance it absorbs far more strongly than dyes and turns light into heat.
  • Gold is easily functionalised through Au-S bonds (PEG, antibodies, drugs, dyes).

Targeting

  • Passive: PEG-coated particles of 100 to 200 nm escape phagocytes and circulate long; leaky, poorly drained tumour vessels trap them (enhanced permeability and retention).
  • Active: antibodies on the shell (for example anti-HER2) bind receptors over-expressed on cancer cells.

Destruction

  1. The site is irradiated with an NIR laser (about 800 nm, a few W cm^{-2}, minutes).
  2. The plasmon absorbs; electrons pass the energy to the lattice in picoseconds, and the nanoshells heat their surroundings.
  3. Above about 42 to 45 °C cells die by hyperthermia (protein denaturation, membrane damage, apoptosis), above about 50 °C by necrosis; only tissue with bound nanoshells gets this hot.
  4. Heat can also release a carried drug, and the particles image the tumour.
pts: Describes the nanoshell: silica (dielectric) core with a thin gold shell; plasmon resonance tuned by the core-to-shell ratio into the NIR
Explains the NIR choice: tissue window (about 650 to 900 nm), low absorption by blood and water, deep penetration, healthy cells not heated
States the nanoshell's roles: strong absorber that converts light to heat, easily functionalised gold surface, carrier for a drug or dye
Passive targeting: PEG stealth, size below about 200 nm, leaky tumour vessels and poor drainage (EPR) make nanoshells accumulate
Active targeting: antibodies bind receptors over-expressed on cancer cells
Destruction: NIR irradiation, plasmon absorption, local heating above about 42 to 45 °C, protein denaturation and membrane damage, only where nanoshells are bound
Heat-triggered drug release or simultaneous imaging (theranostics)
Gives the sequence: inject, accumulate and bind, irradiate, heat and kill

• The NIR light must pass through healthy tissue harmlessly; this is why solid gold (520 nm) is not used: tissue absorbs visible light.
  • Temperature thresholds vary with exposure time; quote "above about 42 °C" for hyperthermia rather than a single number.
  • The nanoshell sizes are typical published values; the slides give only the structure.

6a.html:
All three have a valence band (VB) and a conduction band (CB); they differ in the gap and in where the Fermi energy lies. At 0 K all states below E_F are full and all above are empty; at T > 0,

f(E) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp[(E - E_F)/k_BT]}, \qquad f(E_F) = \tfrac{1}{2}

Conduction needs empty states within about k_BT (0.026 eV at 300 K) of the filled ones.

ConductorSemiconductorInsulator
Bandspartly filled band or overlapping VB and CB (Na: half-full 3s)full VB, empty CBfull VB, empty CB
Gapnonesmall, about 1 eV (Si 1.14 eV)large, above about 4 eV (SiO_2 8.4 eV)
E_Finside a bandnear mid-gapmid-gap
Conductionhigha few electrons excited across the gap; rises with Tnegligible
pts: Conductor: partly filled or overlapping bands with E_F inside a band, so empty states lie just above full ones and it conducts
Semiconductor: small gap (about 1 eV, for example Si) with E_F near mid-gap; thermal excitation gives a few carriers, so conductivity rises with T
Insulator: wide gap (above about 4 eV, for example \mathrm{SiO_2}), E_F mid-gap, negligible carriers
Fermi function: f(E_F) = 1/2, full below E_F at 0 K; conduction needs empty states within about k_BT of E_F

  • The boundary between semiconductor and insulator is a matter of degree: diamond (5.5 eV) is an insulator, GaN (3.4 eV) a wide-gap semiconductor.

6b.html:
The Wulff construction predicts the equilibrium (thermodynamically controlled) shape of a crystal: the shape with the minimum total surface energy \sum_i \gamma_i A_i at fixed volume. Different facets have different surface energies \gamma_i, so this minimum is a faceted polyhedron, not a sphere.

Construction. From a centre, draw a vector along the normal of each facet with length proportional to its \gamma_i. Draw a plane normal to each vector at its tip. The innermost envelope of these planes is the crystal shape. This is the Wulff theorem,

\frac{\gamma_i}{h_i} = \text{constant}

where h_i is the distance of facet i from the centre. High-energy faces therefore expose little or no area, and low-energy (close-packed) faces dominate.

Significance for nanoparticles

  • A nanoparticle has a high surface-to-volume ratio, so surface energy is a large part of its total energy and the facet energies set its shape.
  • It predicts the exposed facets: fcc Au, Ag and Pt nanoparticles form truncated octahedra (cuboctahedra in small clusters) bounded mainly by {111} and {100} facets, with little or no {110}.
  • The exposed facets fix the properties: catalytic activity, plasmon colour and stability.
  • Shape control: a reagent or capping agent that adsorbs on one facet lowers its \gamma. Hydroxylamine gives {100} gold cubes, citric acid {111} gold plates.

Limits. Wulff shapes assume thermodynamic control. Kinetics (fast-growing faces vanish), the roughening temperature (above it facets round off) and, in tiny clusters, edge energy and twinning (icosahedra) cause departures.
pts: Defines the Wulff shape as the equilibrium shape that minimises \sum \gamma_i A_i at constant volume (thermodynamic control)
Describes the construction: vectors proportional to \gamma_i, planes normal to them at their tips, inner envelope; \gamma_i/h_i = constant
States that high-energy faces are small or absent and low-energy faces dominate, with a sketch of a Wulff plot and its shape
Predicts fcc metal nanoparticles as truncated octahedra (cuboctahedra) with {111} and {100} facets
Links the shape to properties (catalysis, plasmon colour) and to shape control by adsorbates that lower one facet's energy
States the limits: kinetic growth control, roughening temperature, edge energy and twinning in very small clusters

• The vector length is proportional to the surface energy, so the longest vectors give the smallest faces. Reversing this is the commonest slip.
  • In the two-dimensional case the {11} facets appear only while \gamma_{11}/\gamma_{10} < \sqrt{2}, and the shape is all {11} when \gamma_{11}/\gamma_{10} \le 1/\sqrt{2}.
  • "Discuss" needs both sides: what the Wulff shape predicts and why real nanocrystals often depart from it.

6c.html:
A grain boundary is the interface between two grains (crystals of the same phase) with different orientations. It is a region about 0.5 to 1 nm wide in which the atoms are misfitted, so it carries an excess energy. Low-angle boundaries (below about 15^\circ) are arrays of dislocations; high-angle boundaries are disordered.

In nanomaterials the boundaries take up a large volume fraction, about 3\delta/d for a boundary width \delta: with \delta = 1 nm, about 3% at d = 100 nm but roughly 30% at d = 10 nm.

Hall-Petch strengthening. Slip planes change orientation across a boundary, so dislocations pile up against it until the stress at the head of the pile-up starts slip in the next grain. Smaller grains hold shorter pile-ups, so a larger applied stress is needed:

\sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k\,d^{-1/2}

where \sigma_0 is the lattice friction stress and k the Hall-Petch slope. For Cu (\sigma_0 \approx 25 MPa, k \approx 0.11\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}), refining d from 10 µm to 100 nm raises \sigma_y from about 60 to about 370 MPa. Grain refinement also improves toughness.

Inverse Hall-Petch below about 10 to 30 nm. Grains become too small to hold a pile-up or a dislocation source. Grain-boundary sliding, grain rotation and boundary diffusion take over, so the strength peaks and then falls, and ductility drops: the slides note that below about 30 nm materials may become brittle. The high boundary energy also drives grain growth, so nanograins must be stabilised by solute segregation or particle pinning.
pts: Defines a grain boundary as the interface between differently oriented grains, a 0.5 to 1 nm misfit region with excess energy (low- and high-angle types)
Notes the large boundary volume fraction in nanomaterials, about 3\delta/d (roughly 30% at 10 nm)
Explains that boundaries block slip, so dislocations pile up and smaller grains need a higher stress to pass slip on
Writes \sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k\,d^{-1/2} with its symbols: strength rises as the grain size falls
States the breakdown below about 10 to 30 nm: no pile-ups, boundary sliding, rotation and diffusion, inverse Hall-Petch and lower ductility
Mentions the grain-growth instability of nanograins, or draws \sigma_y against grain size with the peak

6d.html:
Principle. A crystal diffracts at the Bragg angle, n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta. In a large crystal thousands of planes cancel each other just off \theta_B, so the peak is sharp. A nanocrystal has too few planes for full cancellation, so the peak broadens as the size falls:

D = \frac{K\lambda}{\beta\cos\theta}

D = mean crystallite size normal to the diffracting planes, K \approx 0.9 (shape factor), \lambda = X-ray wavelength, \beta = FWHM in radians, \theta = Bragg angle (half the 2\theta position).

Procedure

  1. Record the pattern (Cu K\alpha, \lambda = 0.15406 nm) and index the phase.
  2. Fit a strong, isolated peak after removing background and K\alpha_2; read 2\theta_B and the FWHM.
  3. Remove instrumental broadening, measured on a coarse standard (LaB_6 or Si): \beta^2 = \beta_m^2 - \beta_i^2 for Gaussian peaks.
  4. Convert \beta to radians, take \theta = 2\theta_B/2, calculate D; average several peaks.

Worked example (ZnO (101) peak, as in the slide pattern; widths assumed): 2\theta = 36.25^\circ, \beta_m = 0.40^\circ, \beta_i = 0.10^\circ.

\begin{aligned} \beta &= \sqrt{0.40^2 - 0.10^2} = 0.387^\circ = 6.76\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}, \qquad \cos 18.125^\circ = 0.950 \\ D &= \frac{0.9 \times 0.15406\ \mathrm{nm}}{(6.76\times10^{-3})(0.950)} = 21.6\ \mathrm{nm} \end{aligned}

Answer: D \approx 22 nm (21 nm without the instrumental correction).

Limits. D is the coherent domain size, not the particle size (a polycrystalline particle gives less). It works for about 2 to 100 nm; larger sizes hide in the instrumental width. Microstrain also broadens peaks; a Williamson-Hall plot, \beta\cos\theta = K\lambda/D + 4\varepsilon\sin\theta, separates the two.
pts: States that finite crystallite size broadens the diffraction peak: fewer planes, incomplete cancellation away from \theta_B; smaller size, broader peak
Writes D = K\lambda/(\beta\cos\theta) and defines every symbol: K \approx 0.9, \beta = FWHM in radians, \theta = Bragg angle
Gives the procedure: fit a strong peak, read 2\theta_B and the FWHM after background and K\alpha_2 removal
Subtracts instrumental broadening measured on a standard (LaB_6 or Si)
Worked number with units, for example D \approx 22 nm for \beta = 0.39^\circ at 2\theta = 36.25^\circ
States the limits: crystallite (domain) size not particle size, valid to about 100 nm, strain broadening (Williamson-Hall)

7a(i).html:
Given: Ti film by PVD, deposition rate R_d = 10\ \mathrm{nm\,s^{-1}}, required thickness d = 500\ \mathrm{nm}.

Find: the deposition time t.

Solution. At a constant rate the thickness grows linearly with time, d = R_d\,t:

t = \frac{d}{R_d} = \frac{500\ \mathrm{nm}}{10\ \mathrm{nm\,s^{-1}}} = 50\ \mathrm{s}

The rate corresponds to an arrival flux, from R_d = F_{\mathrm{dep}}M/(N_{\mathrm{Av}}\rho) with the data of part (ii):

F_{\mathrm{dep}} = \frac{R_d N_{\mathrm{Av}}\rho}{M} = \frac{(1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}})(6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}})(4.51\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}})}{47.867\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}} = 5.7\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}

With an atomic spacing of about 0.26 nm, this is about 38 atomic layers per second.

Answer: t = 50\ \mathrm{s}, assuming a constant rate from the moment the shutter opens, every arriving atom sticking and bulk density.
pts: Uses d = R_d t (thickness equals rate times time) at a constant rate
t = 500\ \mathrm{nm}/(10\ \mathrm{nm\,s^{-1}}) = 50\ \mathrm{s}, with the unit
States the assumptions: constant rate, unit sticking, bulk density
Links the rate to the arrival flux, F_{\mathrm{dep}} = R_d N_{\mathrm{Av}}\rho/M \approx 5.7\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}

7a(ii).html:
Given: uniform Ti film, d = 500\ \mathrm{nm} = 5.00\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}, \rho = 4.51\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}, M = 47.867\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}, N_{\mathrm{Av}} = 6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}.

Find: the number of Ti atoms per \mathrm{cm^2}.

Solution. A film of area A has volume Ad, mass \rho A d and \rho A d/M moles, so per unit area

\begin{aligned} \frac{N}{A} &= \frac{\rho\, d\, N_{\mathrm{Av}}}{M} \\ \rho d &= (4.51\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}})(5.00\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}) = 2.255\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}} \\ \frac{\rho d}{M} &= \frac{2.255\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}}}{47.867\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}} = 4.711\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\,cm^{-2}} \\ \frac{N}{A} &= (4.711\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\,cm^{-2}})(6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}) = 2.84\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}} \end{aligned}

Check: the atom density is \rho N_{\mathrm{Av}}/M = 5.67\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}; times 5.00\times10^{-5} cm it gives the same number, which also equals the flux of part (i) times 50 s.

Answer: N/A \approx 2.84\times10^{18} Ti atoms per \mathrm{cm^2} (a mass of 0.23 mg per \mathrm{cm^2}, about 1900 atomic layers).
pts: Converts the thickness to the length unit of the density: 500 nm = 5.00\times10^{-5} cm
Correct relation N/A = \rho d N_{\mathrm{Av}}/M (mass per area, then moles, then atoms)
Intermediate values 2.255\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}} and 4.71\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\,cm^{-2}}
Final answer 2.84\times10^{18} atoms \mathrm{cm^{-2}}, with units

7b.html:
PVD makes a film in three physical steps: a vapour is generated from a solid source, it travels through vacuum or a low-pressure gas, and it condenses on the substrate. Evaporation and sputtering are the two ways of generating the vapour.

Role of sputtering

  • Vapour source. The target is the cathode (−), the substrate and chamber the anode. After pump-down, Ar is admitted to 1 to 100 mTorr and a glow discharge forms. \mathrm{Ar^+} ions accelerated across the cathode sheath knock target atoms out by momentum transfer (a collision cascade), not by heating (slide 2).
  • Yield and rate. S = atoms ejected per ion, zero below a threshold of 10 to 30 eV, about 2 for Al and 0.9 for Ti at 1 keV (slide 8); R_{\mathrm{dep}} \propto I_{\mathrm{disch}}S.
  • The atoms leave over a range of angles with 3 to 10 eV and travel "ballistically, with some collisions" to the substrate.
  • The same ions also sputter-clean the substrate before deposition, and with bias densify the growing film; with \mathrm{N_2} or \mathrm{O_2} added, reactive sputtering gives TiN or oxides.
  • Uses: Al and Cu seed layers, TiN and TaN barriers, Ti and Ta adhesion layers, silicides (slide 16, printed 18).

How it differs from evaporation

EvaporationSputtering
Vapour generationthermal: R_e \propto p_{\mathrm{eq}}(T_{\mathrm{sor}}), source meltedmomentum transfer; target solid and water-cooled
Pressure, transport10^{-6} to 10^{-10} Torr, \lambda \gg H, line of sight1 to 100 mTorr Ar, some gas collisions
Sourcesmall, hot point or small-area sourcelarge target: wide arrival angles, better step coverage and uniformity
Arrival energyabout kT_{\mathrm{sor}}, 0.1 to 0.2 eV3 to 10 eV: denser, better-adhering films
Materialsneeds a usable vapour pressure; alloys fractionate, compounds dissociatealmost any material; film = target composition; insulators by RF
Purity, structurepurest; epitaxy possible (MBE)Ar and gas incorporated, subsurface damage; poly or amorphous, not epitaxy

Conclusion. Sputtering is the production PVD process for alloys, compounds, refractory metals and adherent, conformal metallisation; evaporation is chosen for the highest purity, lift-off patterning and epitaxial (MBE) growth.
pts: Defines PVD as vapour generation, transport and condensation, with evaporation and sputtering as the two vapour sources
Sputtering mechanism: target as cathode in an Ar glow discharge at 1 to 100 mTorr; \mathrm{Ar^+} ejects atoms by momentum transfer (collision cascade)
Sputter yield S (atoms per ion), threshold 10 to 30 eV, and rate proportional to discharge current times yield
Other roles: substrate sputter-cleaning or bias densification, reactive sputtering of compounds, or industrial uses (Al, Cu, TiN, TaN)
Contrast in vapour generation: thermal evaporation set by p_{\mathrm{eq}}(T_{\mathrm{sor}}) against momentum transfer from a cool target
Contrast in pressure and source: high-vacuum line of sight from a small source against mTorr Ar and an extended target, giving better step coverage
Contrast in arrival energy: 0.1 to 0.2 eV against 3 to 10 eV, so sputtered films are denser and adhere better
Contrast in materials: sputtering keeps alloy composition and handles refractory metals and (with RF) insulators; evaporation fractionates alloys and dissociates compounds
Evaporated films are purer and can be epitaxial (MBE); sputtered films hold Ar and subsurface damage

7b.watch:
• "Role of sputtering in PVD" means the vapour-generation step; do not describe it as a chemical process. Reactive sputtering adds a reaction at the target and film, but the vapour is still made by momentum transfer.
  • The slide 8 yields are read off a plot at 1 keV (Al about 1.95, Ti about 0.85); quote them as approximate.
  • Rates: simple diode sputtering gives only a few hundred Å/min for many metals, a magnetron about 1 μm/min for Al (Ohring), while evaporation rates rise exponentially with T_{\mathrm{sor}}.

8a.html:
Principle (EDAX). The beam ejects an inner-shell (K, L, M) electron; an outer electron fills the hole and emits a characteristic X-ray whose energy identifies the element (Moseley: \sqrt{\nu} \propto Z - 1). An energy-dispersive detector (Si(Li) or silicon drift) sorts the photons into a spectrum of counts against keV.

Procedure

  1. Prepare: disperse particles thinly on a clean conducting substrate (Si wafer, TEM grid); carbon-coat insulators, never gold-coat.
  2. Locate: SE image for shape, BSE image for Z contrast (heavier particles brighter).
  3. Voltage: E_0 about twice the line's critical energy, but low: the interaction volume (4.7 µm deep in Si at 20 kV, 0.5 µm at 5 kV) dwarfs a 50 nm particle. Use low-energy lines (Au M\alpha 2.12 keV, not L\alpha 9.71 keV).
  4. Acquire: spot spectrum, line scan or elemental map (core-shell or alloy distribution).
  5. Analyse: identify peaks, check overlaps (Si K\alpha 1.74, W M\alpha 1.77 keV), subtract the substrate spectrum, quantify by ZAF correction in wt% and at%.

Limits: about 0.1 wt% detection, 130 eV resolution, no H to Li, semi-quantitative on small particles; below about 50 nm use STEM-EDS.
pts: Explains characteristic X-ray emission: inner-shell ionisation, outer electron fills the vacancy, photon energy unique to the element
Detector sorts photons by energy into a counts-against-energy spectrum (Si(Li) or SDD)
Sample preparation: thin dispersion on a clean conducting substrate; carbon coat, not gold
Uses SE and BSE images to find the particle (BSE Z contrast)
Chooses the accelerating voltage: overvoltage about 2, and low kV because the interaction volume (micrometres) exceeds the particle
Spot, line-scan or mapping modes; peak identification with overlaps checked
Quantifies with ZAF correction and states the limits: about 0.1 wt%, no H to Li, substrate signal, semi-quantitative on small particles

  • The interaction depths are from the Kanaya-Okayama range, R = 0.0276\,A E_0^{1.67}/(Z^{0.89}\rho) in µm, with E_0 in keV and \rho in \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.
  • WDS (slide 33) resolves overlapping peaks better but is slower; mention it as the remedy for overlaps.

8b(i).html:
Given: a spherical gold nanoparticle, D = 10 nm (r = 5 nm).

Find: the surface area to volume ratio.

Solution

\begin{aligned} A &= 4\pi r^2 = \pi D^2 = \pi\,(10\ \mathrm{nm})^2 = 314.2\ \mathrm{nm^2} \\ V &= \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{\pi D^3}{6} = \frac{\pi\,(10\ \mathrm{nm})^3}{6} = 523.6\ \mathrm{nm^3} \\ \frac{A}{V} &= \frac{3}{r} = \frac{6}{D} = \frac{314.2\ \mathrm{nm^2}}{523.6\ \mathrm{nm^3}} = 0.6\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} \end{aligned}

In SI units, 0.6\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{nm\,m^{-1}} = 6\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} (6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}).

Answer: A/V = 0.6\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} = 6\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}. A 1 cm sphere has 6\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}, so the nanoparticle has 10^{6} times more surface per unit volume, and about 16% of its atoms sit on the surface.
pts: Surface area \pi D^2 = 314.2\ \mathrm{nm^2} and volume \pi D^3/6 = 523.6\ \mathrm{nm^3}
Shows A/V = 3/r = 6/D
Final answer 0.6\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}, that is 6\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}, with units
Comments on the size: 10^{6} times a 1 cm sphere, or a large fraction of surface atoms

8b(ii).html:
Given: D = 10 nm, \rho_{\mathrm{Au}} = 19.3\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}; from part (i), V = 523.6\ \mathrm{nm^3}.

Find: the mass of one nanoparticle.

Solution

\begin{aligned} 1\ \mathrm{nm} &= 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 1\ \mathrm{nm^3} = 10^{-21}\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ V &= 523.6\ \mathrm{nm^3} = 5.236\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ m &= \rho V = (19.3\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}})(5.236\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{cm^3}) = 1.01\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{g} \end{aligned}

Answer: m \approx 1.0\times10^{-17} g = 1.0\times10^{-20} kg (about 10 attograms). Dividing by the mass of one Au atom, 196.97/(6.022\times10^{23}) = 3.27\times10^{-22} g, gives about 3.1\times10^{4} atoms in the particle.
pts: Volume \pi D^3/6 = 523.6\ \mathrm{nm^3} (carried from part i)
Converts with 1\ \mathrm{nm^3} = 10^{-21}\ \mathrm{cm^3}: V = 5.24\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{cm^3}
Uses m = \rho V
Final answer m \approx 1.01\times10^{-17} g (1.01\times10^{-20} kg), with units

• The commonest slip is the unit conversion: 1\ \mathrm{nm} = 10^{-7} cm, so 1\ \mathrm{nm^3} = 10^{-21}\ \mathrm{cm^3}, not 10^{-9} or 10^{-27}.
  • Slide 40 lists about 17,900 atoms for a "10 nm" Au particle. That number comes from the magic-number cluster formula N = \tfrac{1}{3}(10n^3 - 15n^2 + 11n - 3) for a cuboctahedron 10 nm across its corners (n = 18), which holds less volume than a 10 nm sphere. The full sphere has about 3.1\times10^{4} atoms.

8c.fix: • Slide 36 of 405-L1 says a 10 nm particle has about 15% surface atoms and a 50 nm particle about 6%. For a one-atom surface shell the fraction falls as 1/D, so 15% at 10 nm implies about 3% at 50 nm: for gold (atomic diameter 0.288 nm) the shell gives 16% at 10 nm and 3.4% at 50 nm, and the magic-number cluster formulas of slide 39 give the same.
8c.html:
Why it matters. For a sphere S/V = 3/r = 6/D, so the ratio rises tenfold for every tenfold fall in size: 0.6\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} at 10 nm against 6\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} (6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}) for a 1 cm sphere. The fraction of atoms on the surface rises with it, to about 15% at 10 nm and 92% for a 13-atom cluster. Surface atoms have fewer neighbours and dangling bonds, so they have higher energy and are more reactive. When they are a large fraction of the material:

  1. Reactivity and adsorption scale with the area per gram, 6/(\rho D): about 31\ \mathrm{m^2\,g^{-1}} for 10 nm gold. Catalytic and sensing activity rise sharply.
  2. Thermal properties change. Surface energy is a large part of the total, so the melting point falls. The slide's T_m \approx T_{m,\mathrm{bulk}}(1 - 1/D), with D in nm, gives about 1200 K for 10 nm gold against 1337 K for bulk gold. Sintering starts at lower temperatures too.
  3. Surface forces dominate bulk forces. Van der Waals adhesion between two atoms (about 1.6 pN) far exceeds gravity, so nanoparticles stick together.
  4. Drawbacks: agglomeration and Ostwald ripening, fast oxidation (fine metal powders can ignite) and easy uptake into cells.

Application 1: heterogeneous catalysis. Pt, Pd and Rh particles of 1 to 5 nm on porous alumina in automobile catalytic converters, and Pt on carbon in fuel cells, expose most of their atoms, so far less precious metal gives the same activity. Gold, inert in bulk, oxidises CO as particles below about 5 nm.

Application 2: photocatalysis. \mathrm{TiO_2} nanoparticles absorb UV and create electron-hole pairs that oxidise organic dirt and pollutants at their large surface: self-cleaning glass, air purification and water treatment.

Other uses: \mathrm{SnO_2} gas sensors, supercapacitor and battery electrodes, zeolite filters and drug carriers.
pts: States S/V = 3/r = 6/D, rising as size falls, with a number (for example 0.6\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} at 10 nm against 6\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} for 1 cm)
Larger fraction of surface atoms (about 15% at 10 nm), which have dangling bonds, higher energy and higher reactivity
Reactivity, adsorption and catalytic or sensing activity scale with the specific surface area
Melting-point depression, T_m \approx T_{m,\mathrm{bulk}}(1 - 1/D), or lower sintering temperature, from the surface energy
Surface forces (van der Waals) dominate bulk forces; drawbacks such as agglomeration, oxidation or toxicity
First application explained through surface atoms: catalysis (converters, fuel cells, nano-gold for CO oxidation)
Second application explained: \mathrm{TiO_2} photocatalysis, or gas sensors, electrodes, filters or drug carriers
Concludes that the surface, not the bulk, governs the properties at the nanoscale
